title: Daisy Turns Three
author: Chris Martin
summary: Chris Martin marks his younger daughter Daisy's third birthday with a short reflection written through a bad cold and a hectic September. He begins with gratitude that Daisy, unlike her older sister Maggie born in April 2020, arrived into a world where the family could raise a baby in open community rather than under pandemic restrictions. He then sketches the sisters' different temperaments through their Disney princess affinities: Maggie drawn to the stately princesses, Daisy to adventurers like Moana, Merida and above all Rapunzel, whose Tangled theme will shape her party. Two vignettes carry the piece: Daisy dancing unaware to Stevie Wonder and singing Aretha Franklin, and a thunderstorm drive that became a lesson in cardinal directions and led to her question about storms from the wild west. Martin closes by resisting the urge to typecast his daughters while admitting he pictures Daisy as a fearless athlete, still wearing a dress. It is a fatherhood piece about attention to a particular child.
points: Martin contrasts raising a baby in community with the isolation of parenting his first daughter during the 2020 pandemic.
He uses the girls' Disney princess preferences as a shorthand for their different temperaments rather than as stereotypes.
Exposing his daughters to older music is a deliberate parenting goal, and it produces the piece's most vivid moments with Daisy.
An impromptu driveway lesson on cardinal directions shows everyday teaching folded into bedtime logistics.
quotes: By God’s grace, she was born into a world that was not reeling from a worldwide pandemic, unlike Maggie who was born in April 2020.
Daisy has always seemed to have more of an affinity for the princesses who get their dresses dirty amid dangerous adventure—Moana, Merida, and most of all, Rapunzel.
We listen to a lot of music in our house, and it’s a goal of mine to expose our girls to lots of different kinds of music as they grow up.
And she said, “I just movin’!” seemingly unaware of the fact that she had been caught up in the music.
Sitting on the glider looking for birds, Daisy said, “Daddy, are the storms still going to come from the wild west?
I often think about what our girls will be like when they get older, while resisting the temptation to pigeon-hole or typecast them.
